metadata.title: Advanced programming language concepts (LINFO1131)
metadata.description:
Advanced programming language concepts (LINFO1131) is a third-year university course given to all computer science majors at the École Polytechnique de Louvain (UCLouvain Engineering School).  LINFO1131 is a successor course to LINFO1104 also given at EPL. Note that the course LINGI1131 is an earlier course that later became LINFO1131. Part of this course, Lectures 1 through 5, give a comprehensive presentation of declarative programming: what it is, why it is powerful, and what are its limitations. Table of contents:
1. Refresher of previous course (LINFO1104). Summary of Oz, higher-order programming, symbolic programming, deterministic dataflow concurrency, nondeterminism, and semantics.
2. Lazy evaluation, lazy deterministic dataflow, lazy quicksort. How lazy evaluation can use infinite data structures and invent incremental algorithms.
3. What is declarative programming? All executions reach partial termination and give logically equivalent stores.
4. Advanced declarative algorithm design. Single assignment supports fast ephemeral algorithms and lazy evaluation supports fast persistent algorithms.
5. Limitations of declarative programming.  Programs that interact with the real world are not declarative.
6. Data abstractions.  Objects and abstract data types, which each can be purely functional or stateful.
7. Message-passing concurrency and multi-agent programming.  How to design programs as networks of active objects that pass messages.
8. Robust multi-agent programming in Erlang.  Basic concepts of Erlang and high-level abstractions (behaviors) that support robust multi-agent applications using the “let it crash” approach.
9. Shared-state concurrency. How to design concurrent programs that share state by building large atomic actions, namely locks and tuple spaces.
10. Monitors.  How threads can collaborate in shared-state programs.  Monitors are widely used in legacy code but are a deprecated concept.
11. Transactions.  How to build robust high-performance databases with abortable atomic actions.

metadata.title: Compiler Principles
metadata.description:
Compilers Principles (Course Code: 19041382)
Welcome to the Compilers Principles course offered by the College of Information Technology – Department of Computer Science at Palestine Technical University – Kadoorie (PTUK).
Taught by Dr. Eman Yaser Daraghmi, this lecture is part of the Bachelor of Computer Science program for the academic year 2024–2025 (Second Semester).

- About the Course
Compilers Principles explores the fundamental syntactic and semantic elements of modern programming languages and the computational models that define them.
Students learn the algorithms and techniques used by compilers to translate high-level programming languages into machine code and other target representations.

This course covers:

- Lexical Analysis

- Syntax and Semantic Analysis

- Syntax-Directed Translation

- Intermediate Code Generation

- Code Optimization and Code Generation

By the end of the course, students will be able to:

- Understand the structure and phases of a compiler

- Apply compiler-construction tools such as Lex and YACC

- Design syntax trees and generate three-address code

- Integrate compiler phases into a working mini-compiler
